Further, the presentation in the impact statement assumes that traffic volume to and from the airport will remain constant with or without the Airport Spur. Numerous studies throughout the country demonstrate that additional highway facilities attract and encourage increased traffic. The impact statement does not assume this and therefore must be corrected before an adequate assessment of the impact on air quality can be made.4
Finally, the impact state presents the quantities of air pollution emissions in Tons/day rather than in lbs. particulate/million (ppm). This makes it difficult for the average citizen to determine how close to compliance the predicted emissions will be to the primary and secondary standards. This too must be corrected before a judgement can be made on the net effect to air quality that the proposed project will have.5
Only after these oversights are corrected can an adequate assessment of the impact of the project on the air quality in the area be made.
Noise
It is clear form the evidence presented by the Division of Highways that the Airport Spur will cause a degradation in the noise quality. In figure 13 on page 100 at the site of the Hamlin Garland School, site 15, the predicted noise levels by 1990 will exceed the approved limits. The fact that this is the site of an educational institution makes this situation ever-more critical.
Given that the proposed Airport Spur will clash with many societal goals and potentially clash with others, it is time to consider alternatives to constructing the Airport Spur.
Alternatives
I have identified three justifications for construction of the Airport Spur:
1. To decrease travel time between two interstate facilities.
2. To meet the projected demands for air and ground transportation.
3. To provide greater travelling safety.
I believe that all three of these goals can be met without constructing this 12.1 million, 1.5 mile interstate type facility.
An attractive alternative has been proposed by State Representative John Plewa.
